Limits — JEE Main revision guide

A limit asks: where do the output values go when the input moves closer and closer? It does not ask us to divide by zero.

Scope and prerequisites before studying

The official Mathematics Unit 7 includes limits and graphs of simple functions. We cover the needed algebraic, trigonometric, exponential and logarithmic limits, plus the sequence limits in the supplied questions.

  • Angles in these limits are in radians.
  • A short derivative-definition lesson is included for Q15. That question assumes differentiability only at one point.
  • Q10 and Q11 need the idea of a sum of thin rectangle areas. Its meaning and the two area formulas needed here are explained locally.
  • Expansions and L'Hôpital's rule are supporting methods. They are taught with conditions, not as replacements for understanding the basic limits.
  • Initial independent calculations agree with the intended source answers. Domains, one-sided signs and cancellation orders still need care.

Formula and concept bank

Concept C01 — A limit is a nearby-output question

Think of xxx as an input to a machine and f(x)f(x)f(x) as its output. The statement

lim⁡x→af(x)=L\boxed{\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L}x→alim​f(x)=L​

means: by taking allowed inputs sufficiently close to aaa, but different from aaa, we can make the outputs as close as we want to LLL.

The input approaches aaa; the output approaches LLL. The number f(a)f(a)f(a) may be different, or may not be defined.

For example,

f(x)=x2−1x−1=x+1(x≠1).f(x)=\frac{x^2-1}{x-1}=x+1\qquad(x\ne1).f(x)=x−1x2−1​=x+1(x=1).

At x=0.9x=0.9x=0.9, the output is 1.91.91.9; at x=1.1x=1.1x=1.1, it is 2.12.12.1. As xxx moves towards 111, the output moves towards 222. Therefore

lim⁡x→1x2−1x−1=2,\lim_{x\to1}\frac{x^2-1}{x-1}=2,x→1lim​x−1x2−1​=2,

even though the displayed fraction has no value at x=1x=1x=1.

Read the picture: the hollow dot is the missing value on the line. A filled dot shows a separately assigned value. The limit follows the nearby line, not the isolated filled dot.

The formal “as close as we want” idea is stronger than looking at a few decimal inputs. A graph and a table help us guess; an identity, bound or theorem proves the limit.

Concept C02 — Check left, right and the allowed inputs

The left-hand limit uses x<ax<ax<a; the right-hand limit uses x>ax>ax>a:

lim⁡x→a−f(x),lim⁡x→a+f(x).\lim_{x\to a^-}f(x),\qquad \lim_{x\to a^+}f(x).x→a−lim​f(x),x→a+lim​f(x).

For an ordinary two-sided finite limit at an interior point,

lim⁡x→af(x)=L  ⟺  left limit=right limit=L.\boxed{\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L \iff \text{left limit}=\text{right limit}=L.}x→alim​f(x)=L⟺left limit=right limit=L.​

For ∣x∣/x|x|/x∣x∣/x, the output is −1-1−1 on the left and 111 on the right. Both side limits exist, but they differ, so the two-sided limit does not exist.

Important for JEE Main: modulus, greatest-integer and piecewise functions often require this side check before any formula.

Remember the real domains:

  • ln⁡u\ln ulnu needs u>0u>0u>0.
  • u\sqrt uu​ needs u≥0u\ge0u≥0.
  • A denominator must not be zero at the nearby inputs used.
  • A general real power uvu^vuv is safely defined through evln⁡ue^{v\ln u}evlnu when u>0u>0u>0.

At an endpoint, approach through the allowed domain. For example, x\sqrt xx​ near 000 has a right-hand approach in its real domain. Do not invent a left real branch.

If outputs grow beyond every positive bound, we write a limit +∞+\infty+∞; this is not a finite real value. Likewise for −∞-\infty−∞. If the sides give opposite infinities, there is no common two-sided infinite limit.

Concept C03 — Try substitution; then name what is unresolved

If f,gf,gf,g have finite limits A,BA,BA,B, then

lim⁡(f+g)=A+B,lim⁡(fg)=AB,lim⁡fg=AB if B≠0.\lim(f+g)=A+B,\quad \lim(fg)=AB,\quad \boxed{\lim\frac fg=\frac AB\ \text{if }B\ne0}.lim(f+g)=A+B,lim(fg)=AB,limgf​=BA​ if B=0​.

Polynomials can be evaluated directly at finite inputs. Rational functions can too when the denominator there is nonzero. The standard trigonometric, exponential, logarithmic and root functions are continuous at inputs inside their domains.

What is 0/00/00/0? It says that both numerator and denominator approach zero. It does not tell us which goes to zero faster:

xx=1,x2x=x→0,xx2=1x\frac{x}{x}=1,\quad \frac{x^2}{x}=x\to0,\quad \frac{x}{x^2}=\frac1xxx​=1,xx2​=x→0,x2x​=x1​

have the same 0/00/00/0 substitution pattern but different behaviour.

The forms

00, ∞∞, ∞−∞, 0⋅∞, 1∞, 00, ∞0\boxed{\frac00,\ \frac{\infty}{\infty},\ \infty-\infty,\ 0\cdot\infty,\ 1^\infty,\ 0^0,\ \infty^0}00​, ∞∞​, ∞−∞, 0⋅∞, 1∞, 00, ∞0​

are called indeterminate: the form alone does not decide the answer. Rewrite first.

For composition, if g(x)→bg(x)\to bg(x)→b and FFF is continuous at bbb, then F(g(x))→F(b)F(g(x))\to F(b)F(g(x))→F(b). If FFF has a jump at bbb, check how g(x)g(x)g(x) reaches bbb; direct composition can fail. The floor function in C10 is an example.

Concept C04 — Algebra can remove the apparent zero denominator

Factor and cancel only at nearby nonzero factors.

x2−a2x−a=x+a(x≠a).\frac{x^2-a^2}{x-a}=x+a\qquad(x\ne a).x−ax2−a2​=x+a(x=a).

The equality need not hold at x=ax=ax=a to give the limit there. It holds at all sufficiently close inputs except that one point.

Two square roots or a root minus a number? Try the conjugate.

(A−B)(A+B)=A−B.(\sqrt A-\sqrt B)(\sqrt A+\sqrt B)=A-B.(A​−B​)(A​+B​)=A−B.

For example,

1+x−1x=11+x+1⟶12.\frac{\sqrt{1+x}-1}{x} =\frac1{\sqrt{1+x}+1}\longrightarrow\frac12.x1+x​−1​=1+x​+11​⟶21​.

Cube roots? Use the difference of cubes. If u3=A,v3=Bu^3=A,v^3=Bu3=A,v3=B,

u−v=A−Bu2+uv+v2\boxed{u-v=\frac{A-B}{u^2+uv+v^2}}u−v=u2+uv+v2A−B​​

when the denominator is nonzero. This is the cube-root partner of rationalizing a square root.

A useful general result, for fixed real α\alphaα and 1+t>01+t>01+t>0 near 000, is

lim⁡t→0(1+t)α−1t=α.\boxed{\lim_{t\to0}\frac{(1+t)^\alpha-1}{t}=\alpha.}t→0lim​t(1+t)α−1​=α.​

For integer n≥1n\ge1n≥1,

lim⁡x→axn−anx−a=nan−1.\boxed{\lim_{x\to a}\frac{x^n-a^n}{x-a}=na^{n-1}}.x→alim​x−axn−an​=nan−1​.

It follows by factoring the numerator into x−ax-ax−a times nnn terms, each tending to an−1a^{n-1}an−1. Before using this result, check whether a larger exact factorization already cancels the whole denominator, as in Q8.

Concept C05 — Small angles: the denominator must match the angle

Important for JEE Main. For radians,

lim⁡t→0sin⁡tt=1,lim⁡t→0tan⁡tt=1,lim⁡t→01−cos⁡tt2=12.\boxed{\lim_{t\to0}\frac{\sin t}{t}=1},\qquad \boxed{\lim_{t\to0}\frac{\tan t}{t}=1},\qquad \boxed{\lim_{t\to0}\frac{1-\cos t}{t^2}=\frac12}.t→0lim​tsint​=1​,t→0lim​ttant​=1​,t→0lim​t21−cost​=21​​.

The first says that for a tiny angle the sine height and the angle's numerical value become nearly equal in relative size.

For 0<t<π/20<t<\pi/20<t<π/2, unit-circle area comparisons give

sin⁡t<t<tan⁡t⇒cos⁡t<sin⁡tt<1.\sin t<t<\tan t \quad\Rightarrow\quad \cos t<\frac{\sin t}{t}<1.sint<t<tant⇒cost<tsint​<1.

Both bounds tend to 111. Negative ttt gives the same ratio because sin⁡(−t)/(−t)=sin⁡t/t\sin(-t)/(-t)=\sin t/tsin(−t)/(−t)=sint/t.

Read the drawing: the radius is 111 and the angle is ttt radians. Triangle OABOABOAB, sector OABOABOAB, and triangle OATOATOAT have areas 12sin⁡t\tfrac12\sin t21​sint, 12t\tfrac12t21​t, and 12tan⁡t\tfrac12\tan t21​tant. This is the squeeze behind the first limit.

Then tan⁡t/t=(sin⁡t/t)/cos⁡t→1\tan t/t=(\sin t/t)/\cos t\to1tant/t=(sint/t)/cost→1. Also,

1−cos⁡tt2=2sin⁡2(t/2)t2=12(sin⁡(t/2)t/2)2→12.\frac{1-\cos t}{t^2} =\frac{2\sin^2(t/2)}{t^2} =\frac12\left(\frac{\sin(t/2)}{t/2}\right)^2\to\frac12.t21−cost​=t22sin2(t/2)​=21​(t/2sin(t/2)​)2→21​.

For constants a,ba,ba,b with b≠0b\ne0b=0:

lim⁡x→0sin⁡axsin⁡bx=ab,lim⁡x→01−cos⁡axx2=a22.\boxed{\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin ax}{\sin bx}=\frac ab},\qquad \boxed{\lim_{x\to0}\frac{1-\cos ax}{x^2}=\frac{a^2}{2}}.x→0lim​sinbxsinax​=ba​​,x→0lim​x21−cosax​=2a2​​.

The first also works with tan⁡\tantan in either place. Match the angle first: sin⁡5x/(5x)→1\sin5x/(5x)\to1sin5x/(5x)→1; sin⁡5x/x→5\sin5x/x\to5sin5x/x→5.

Useful exact identities:

tan⁡x−sin⁡x=tan⁡x(1−cos⁡x),3sin⁡x−sin⁡3x=4sin⁡3x,sin⁡(π−u)=sin⁡u.\tan x-\sin x=\tan x(1-\cos x),\quad 3\sin x-\sin3x=4\sin^3x,\quad \sin(\pi-u)=\sin u.tanx−sinx=tanx(1−cosx),3sinx−sin3x=4sin3x,sin(π−u)=sinu.

They can turn a difficult difference into products of standard limits.

Concept C06 — Exponential, logarithmic, root and inverse-trig standards

eee is the natural exponential base, about 2.7182.7182.718. ln⁡\lnln means logarithm to base eee.

Important for JEE Main:

lim⁡t→0et−1t=1,lim⁡t→0at−1t=ln⁡a(a>0),\boxed{\lim_{t\to0}\frac{e^t-1}{t}=1},\quad \boxed{\lim_{t\to0}\frac{a^t-1}{t}=\ln a}\quad(a>0),t→0lim​tet−1​=1​,t→0lim​tat−1​=lna​(a>0), lim⁡t→0ln⁡(1+t)t=1(1+t>0).\boxed{\lim_{t\to0}\frac{\ln(1+t)}{t}=1}\quad(1+t>0).t→0lim​tln(1+t)​=1​(1+t>0).

These are local change-per-input results. Close to zero, et−1e^t-1et−1 and ln⁡(1+t)\ln(1+t)ln(1+t) have leading term ttt.

For a>0,a≠1a>0,a\ne1a>0,a=1, log⁡a(1+t)=ln⁡(1+t)/ln⁡a\log_a(1+t)=\ln(1+t)/\ln aloga​(1+t)=ln(1+t)/lna; its ratio to ttt tends to 1/ln⁡a1/\ln a1/lna.

To use a small inner expression u(x)→0u(x)\to0u(x)→0, factor it explicitly:

eu(x)−1v(x)=eu(x)−1u(x)u(x)v(x).\frac{e^{u(x)}-1}{v(x)} =\frac{e^{u(x)}-1}{u(x)}\frac{u(x)}{v(x)}.v(x)eu(x)−1​=u(x)eu(x)−1​v(x)u(x)​.

The first factor tends to 111; the second carries the actual scale. Handle isolated zeros by the corresponding continuous extension when needed.

Other useful standards in radians are

lim⁡t→0sin⁡−1tt=1,lim⁡t→0tan⁡−1tt=1.\boxed{\lim_{t\to0}\frac{\sin^{-1}t}{t}=1},\qquad \boxed{\lim_{t\to0}\frac{\tan^{-1}t}{t}=1}.t→0lim​tsin−1t​=1​,t→0lim​ttan−1t​=1​.

For the first, put t=sin⁡ut=\sin ut=sinu; then u/sin⁡u→1u/\sin u\to1u/sinu→1 on the principal inverse branch. The second follows by t=tan⁡ut=\tan ut=tanu. Here sin⁡−1\sin^{-1}sin−1 means inverse sine, not 1/sin⁡1/\sin1/sin.

Concept C07 — Expansion: find the first term that survives

An expansion writes a function near zero as a polynomial plus a controlled small remainder. It helps when the question subtracts the earlier terms.

For small real ttt,

et=1+t+t22+t36+t424+t5120+O(t6),sin⁡t=t−t36+t5120+O(t7),cos⁡t=1−t22+t424+O(t6),tan⁡t=t+t33+2t515+O(t7),ln⁡(1+t)=t−t22+t33−t44+t55+O(t6),(1+t)α=1+αt+α(α−1)2t2+α(α−1)(α−2)6t3+O(t4).\begin{aligned} e^t&=1+t+\frac{t^2}{2}+\frac{t^3}{6} +\frac{t^4}{24}+\frac{t^5}{120}+O(t^6),\\ \sin t&=t-\frac{t^3}{6}+\frac{t^5}{120}+O(t^7),\\ \cos t&=1-\frac{t^2}{2}+\frac{t^4}{24}+O(t^6),\\ \tan t&=t+\frac{t^3}{3}+\frac{2t^5}{15}+O(t^7),\\ \ln(1+t)&=t-\frac{t^2}{2}+\frac{t^3}{3} -\frac{t^4}{4}+\frac{t^5}{5}+O(t^6),\\ (1+t)^\alpha&=1+\alpha t+\frac{\alpha(\alpha-1)}2t^2 +\frac{\alpha(\alpha-1)(\alpha-2)}6t^3+O(t^4). \end{aligned}etsintcosttantln(1+t)(1+t)α​=1+t+2t2​+6t3​+24t4​+120t5​+O(t6),=t−6t3​+120t5​+O(t7),=1−2t2​+24t4​+O(t6),=t+3t3​+152t5​+O(t7),=t−2t2​+3t3​−4t4​+5t5​+O(t6),=1+αt+2α(α−1)​t2+6α(α−1)(α−2)​t3+O(t4).​

What does O(tm)O(t^m)O(tm) mean? The remainder has absolute value at most a fixed constant times ∣t∣m|t|^m∣t∣m for sufficiently small ttt. Thus O(t7)/t5=O(t2)→0O(t^7)/t^5=O(t^2)\to0O(t7)/t5=O(t2)→0. It is an error bound, not an extra coefficient to calculate. Logarithm and real-power expansions are used near 000 with 1+t>01+t>01+t>0; the infinite log series is not being asserted for all ttt.

Did you notice the subtraction pattern?

sin⁡x−x+x36=x−x⏟0+(−x36+x36)⏟0+x5120+O(x7).\sin x-x+\frac{x^3}{6} =\underbrace{x-x}_{0} +\underbrace{\left(-\frac{x^3}{6}+\frac{x^3}{6}\right)}_{0} +\frac{x^5}{120}+O(x^7).sinx−x+6x3​=0x−x​​+0(−6x3​+6x3​)​​+120x5​+O(x7).

The denominator x5x^5x5 tells us to keep the fifth-power term. Stopping at sin⁡x≈x\sin x\approx xsinx≈x would erase the very information we need.

Frequently useful results obtained this way:

lim⁡x→0x−sin⁡xx3=16,lim⁡x→0tan⁡x−xx3=13,\boxed{\lim_{x\to0}\frac{x-\sin x}{x^3}=\frac16},\quad \boxed{\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\tan x-x}{x^3}=\frac13},x→0lim​x3x−sinx​=61​​,x→0lim​x3tanx−x​=31​​, lim⁡x→0ex−1−xx2=12,lim⁡x→0ln⁡(1+x)−xx2=−12,\boxed{\lim_{x\to0}\frac{e^x-1-x}{x^2}=\frac12},\quad \boxed{\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\ln(1+x)-x}{x^2}=-\frac12},x→0lim​x2ex−1−x​=21​​,x→0lim​x2ln(1+x)−x​=−21​​, lim⁡x→0ln⁡cos⁡xx2=−12,lim⁡x→01+x−1−x/2x2=−18.\boxed{\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\ln\cos x}{x^2}=-\frac12},\quad \boxed{\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sqrt{1+x}-1-x/2}{x^2}=-\frac18}.x→0lim​x2lncosx​=−21​​,x→0lim​x21+x​−1−x/2​=−81​​.

For example, ln⁡cos⁡x=ln⁡(1+u)\ln\cos x=\ln(1+u)lncosx=ln(1+u) with u=cos⁡x−1=−x2/2+O(x4)u=\cos x-1=-x^2/2+O(x^4)u=cosx−1=−x2/2+O(x4). Since ln⁡(1+u)=u+O(u2)\ln(1+u)=u+O(u^2)ln(1+u)=u+O(u2), the answer follows.

Safe choice rule: exact algebra or a standard-limit product is often shorter. Expand when there is genuine cancellation, and retain enough terms to control what remains after division.

Concept C08 — Variable powers: take the logarithm of the whole expression

Important for JEE Main. A base going to 111 does not force a power to go to 111 when the exponent grows without bound.

Let Y(x)=(1+u(x))v(x)Y(x)=(1+u(x))^{v(x)}Y(x)=(1+u(x))v(x), where u(x)→0u(x)\to0u(x)→0 and the base is positive nearby. Then

ln⁡Y=vln⁡(1+u)=(vu)ln⁡(1+u)u.\ln Y=v\ln(1+u) =(vu)\frac{\ln(1+u)}u.lnY=vln(1+u)=(vu)uln(1+u)​.

If vu→ℓvu\to\ellvu→ℓ, a finite number, the last factor tends to 111. Therefore

(1+u)v⟶eℓif u→0, 1+u>0, vu→ℓ.\boxed{(1+u)^v\longrightarrow e^\ell \quad\text{if }u\to0,\ 1+u>0,\ vu\to\ell.}(1+u)v⟶eℓif u→0, 1+u>0, vu→ℓ.​

In particular,

lim⁡x→∞(1+ax)bx=eab.\boxed{\lim_{x\to\infty}\left(1+\frac ax\right)^{bx}=e^{ab}}.x→∞lim​(1+xa​)bx=eab​.

Understand the balance: the base moves closer to 111, but more and more multiplications can preserve a finite overall change.

For (cos⁡x)1/x2(\cos x)^{1/x^2}(cosx)1/x2, the base is positive for sufficiently small ∣x∣|x|∣x∣. Since

ln⁡Y=ln⁡cos⁡xx2→−12,\ln Y=\frac{\ln\cos x}{x^2}\to-\frac12,lnY=x2lncosx​→−21​,

we get Y→e−1/2Y\to e^{-1/2}Y→e−1/2.

Read the panels: the left graph tracks the easier logarithm; the right takes the exponential back. The holes mark the missing input x=0x=0x=0.

Nested powers need enough accuracy. In Q17 the inner (1+x)1/x(1+x)^{1/x}(1+x)1/x tends to eee, but replacing it by exactly eee too early would lose its small error. The outside exponent 1/x1/x1/x magnifies that error. Take the logarithm of the complete expression first.

The same logarithm idea handles 000^000 and ∞0\infty^0∞0 forms when the base is positive. Analyze vln⁡uv\ln uvlnu; do not declare the answer from the displayed power form alone.

Concept C09 — At infinity, compare sizes and keep signs

For rational functions, divide numerator and denominator by the largest relevant power of xxx:

3x2+2x5x2−7⟶35(x→±∞).\frac{3x^2+2x}{5x^2-7}\longrightarrow\frac35 \quad(x\to\pm\infty).5x2−73x2+2x​⟶53​(x→±∞).

If the numerator has lower degree, the ratio tends to zero. If it has higher degree, inspect the leading power and its sign; a finite limit usually does not result.

A root has an absolute value:

x2=∣x∣,x2+ax+b=∣x∣1+ax+bx2.\boxed{\sqrt{x^2}=|x|,\qquad \sqrt{x^2+ax+b} =|x|\sqrt{1+\frac ax+\frac b{x^2}}.}x2​=∣x∣,x2+ax+b​=∣x∣1+xa​+x2b​​.​

For x→+∞x\to+\inftyx→+∞, ∣x∣=x|x|=x∣x∣=x; for x→−∞x\to-\inftyx→−∞, ∣x∣=−x|x|=-x∣x∣=−x. Forgetting this can reverse an answer.

For a difference of large roots, first rationalize:

x2+ax+b−x2+cx+d=(a−c)x+b−dx2+ax+b+x2+cx+d.\sqrt{x^2+ax+b}-\sqrt{x^2+cx+d} =\frac{(a-c)x+b-d} {\sqrt{x^2+ax+b}+\sqrt{x^2+cx+d}}.x2+ax+b​−x2+cx+d​=x2+ax+b​+x2+cx+d​(a−c)x+b−d​.

As x→+∞x\to+\inftyx→+∞, divide by xxx to obtain (a−c)/2(a-c)/2(a−c)/2. As x→−∞x\to-\inftyx→−∞, the corresponding limit is −(a−c)/2-(a-c)/2−(a−c)/2.

Why “both roots are about xxx” is not enough: it removes the smaller terms whose difference may survive. The conjugate keeps those terms exactly.

A useful size hierarchy, for fixed p>0p>0p>0 and a>1a>1a>1, is

ln⁡xxp→0,xpax→0(x→+∞).\boxed{\frac{\ln x}{x^p}\to0,\qquad \frac{x^p}{a^x}\to0\quad(x\to+\infty)}.xplnx​→0,axxp​→0(x→+∞)​.

Thus tpln⁡t→0t^p\ln t\to0tplnt→0 as t→0+t\to0^+t→0+. This hierarchy compares a logarithm, a positive power and an exponential. Their conditions matter; axa^xax is not a growing exponential when 0<a<10<a<10<a<1.

Concept C10 — Greatest integer: keep a bound on the rounding error

The greatest integer function [t]=⌊t⌋[t]=\lfloor t\rfloor[t]=⌊t⌋ is the largest integer not exceeding ttt. For example, [2.7]=2[2.7]=2[2.7]=2 and [−0.2]=−1[-0.2]=-1[−0.2]=−1.

t−1<[t]≤t.\boxed{t-1<[t]\le t}.t−1<[t]≤t​.

It differs from ttt by less than one. Its graph is a staircase, with a filled left endpoint and a hollow right endpoint on each step.

For Q9, multiply only after checking the sign of xxx. With x>0x>0x>0,

ax−1<[ax]≤ax⇒a−x<x[ax]≤a.\frac ax-1<\left[\frac ax\right]\le\frac ax \quad\Rightarrow\quad \boxed{a-x<x\left[\frac ax\right]\le a}.xa​−1<[xa​]≤xa​⇒a−x<x[xa​]≤a​.

Both bounds tend to aaa as x→0+x\to0^+x→0+. The steps become more frequent, but their vertical error after scaling becomes smaller.

Do not write [a/x]=a/x[a/x]=a/x[a/x]=a/x as an exact equality. The inequality is why the limit still works.

The fractional part is {t}=t−[t]∈[0,1)\{t\}=t-[t]\in[0,1){t}=t−[t]∈[0,1). This notation is useful when isolating the same bounded error.

Concept C11 — Squeeze: a small amplitude can defeat fast oscillation

If A(x)≤f(x)≤B(x)A(x)\le f(x)\le B(x)A(x)≤f(x)≤B(x) near the point and both bounds tend to LLL, then f(x)→Lf(x)\to Lf(x)→L.

Since ∣sin⁡t∣≤1|\sin t|\le1∣sint∣≤1,

∣xsin⁡(1/x)∣≤∣x∣→0⇒xsin⁡(1/x)→0.|x\sin(1/x)|\le|x|\to0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \boxed{x\sin(1/x)\to0}.∣xsin(1/x)∣≤∣x∣→0⇒xsin(1/x)→0​.

But sin⁡(1/x)\sin(1/x)sin(1/x) alone has no limit: inputs

xn=1π/2+2πn,yn=13π/2+2πnx_n=\frac1{\pi/2+2\pi n},\qquad y_n=\frac1{3\pi/2+2\pi n}xn​=π/2+2πn1​,yn​=3π/2+2πn1​

both approach zero while their outputs stay 111 and −1-1−1.

Read the picture: the curve wiggles faster near zero, but every wiggle lies inside a shrinking V-shaped envelope.

More generally, if ggg is bounded nearby and h(x)→0h(x)\to0h(x)→0, then h(x)g(x)→0h(x)g(x)\to0h(x)g(x)→0. A bounded function need not have its own limit for this result.

Recognition clue: an oscillating sine/cosine with a small multiplying factor suggests a bound. L'Hôpital differentiation may make the oscillation worse instead of solving the problem.

Concept C12 — Sequence limits: simplify the finite sum first

For a sequence, nnn approaches infinity through positive integers. If the number of terms grows with nnn, do not take the limit of one fixed term and assume that decides the sum.

A telescoping sum is one in which neighbouring terms cancel. For Q25,

1(2r−1)(2r+1)=12(12r−1−12r+1).\frac1{(2r-1)(2r+1)} =\frac12\left(\frac1{2r-1}-\frac1{2r+1}\right).(2r−1)(2r+1)1​=21​(2r−11​−2r+11​).

Write the finite partial sum before the limit:

Sn=12[(1−13)+(13−15)+⋯+(12n−1−12n+1)]=12(1−12n+1)⟶12.\begin{aligned} S_n&=\frac12\left[(1-\tfrac13) +(\tfrac13-\tfrac15)+\cdots +(\tfrac1{2n-1}-\tfrac1{2n+1})\right]\\ &=\frac12\left(1-\frac1{2n+1}\right) \longrightarrow\frac12. \end{aligned}Sn​​=21​[(1−31​)+(31​−51​)+⋯+(2n−11​−2n+11​)]=21​(1−2n+11​)⟶21​.​

Another common finite sum: 1+q+⋯+qn−1=(1−qn)/(1−q)1+q+\cdots+q^{n-1}=(1-q^n)/(1-q)1+q+⋯+qn−1=(1−qn)/(1−q) for q≠1q\ne1q=1. If ∣q∣<1|q|<1∣q∣<1, then qn→0q^n\to0qn→0 and the sum tends to 1/(1−q)1/(1-q)1/(1−q). For q=1q=1q=1 the sum is nnn; it does not have that finite limit.

Concept C13 — A normalized sum can be an area

Imagine cutting the interval [0,1][0,1][0,1] into nnn equal widths. Each width is Δt=1/n\Delta t=1/nΔt=1/n. Build rectangle rrr with height F(r/n)F(r/n)F(r/n):

total rectangle area=1n∑r=1nF(r/n).\text{total rectangle area} =\frac1n\sum_{r=1}^n F(r/n).total rectangle area=n1​r=1∑n​F(r/n).

For continuous FFF on [0,1][0,1][0,1], the exact area limit is

lim⁡n→∞1n∑r=1nF(r/n)=∫01F(t) dt.\boxed{\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\sum_{r=1}^nF(r/n) =\int_0^1F(t)\,dt}.n→∞lim​n1​r=1∑n​F(r/n)=∫01​F(t)dt​.

The integral sign here means the signed area limit. For our two questions the heights are positive, so it is ordinary area. A dummy letter such as ttt labels position across the rectangles; it is not the original sequence index.

Read the picture: each rectangle contributes width times height. More, thinner rectangles fit the curve more closely. One rectangle becoming thin does not make the sum of all rectangles zero.

The two local facts needed are

∫01dt1+t2=[tan⁡−1t]01=π4,∫01t4 dt=[t5/5]01=15.\int_0^1\frac{dt}{1+t^2} =[\tan^{-1}t]_0^1=\frac\pi4,\qquad \int_0^1t^4\,dt=[t^5/5]_0^1=\frac15.∫01​1+t2dt​=[tan−1t]01​=4π​,∫01​t4dt=[t5/5]01​=51​.

The brackets mean “value at 111 minus value at 000.” These follow from the area/antiderivative connection: the derivatives of tan⁡−1t\tan^{-1}ttan−1t and t5/5t^5/5t5/5 are the displayed heights. Full integration methods belong to their later chapters; only these two facts are needed here.

For a general interval [a,b][a,b][a,b],

b−an∑r=1nF ⁣(a+r(b−a)n)⟶∫abF(t) dt\boxed{\frac{b-a}{n}\sum_{r=1}^n F\!\left(a+\frac{r(b-a)}n\right) \longrightarrow\int_a^bF(t)\,dt}nb−a​r=1∑n​F(a+nr(b−a)​)⟶∫ab​F(t)dt​

when FFF is continuous. Recognition clue: look for a width 1/n1/n1/n or (b−a)/n(b-a)/n(b−a)/n and a changing ratio r/nr/nr/n.

Concept C14 — A derivative is a special limit of slopes

This short prerequisite is needed for Q15. The derivative at aaa is the finite limit

f′(a)=lim⁡h→0f(a+h)−f(a)h.\boxed{f'(a)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}h}.f′(a)=h→0lim​hf(a+h)−f(a)​​.

The numerator is the output change; hhh is the input change. Their ratio is the slope of the line joining two nearby graph points. Its limit is the tangent slope.

If the step is khkhkh, not hhh, keep the scaling:

f(a+kh)−f(a)h⟶kf′(a)\boxed{\frac{f(a+kh)-f(a)}h\longrightarrow kf'(a)}hf(a+kh)−f(a)​⟶kf′(a)​

for fixed kkk when fff is differentiable at aaa. For k≠0k\ne0k=0, insert khkhkh in the denominator and multiply by kkk.

Read the picture: in Q15 the two inputs are 4h4h4h apart. That is why a factor four appears.

For a general numerator f(a+ph)−f(a+qh)f(a+ph)-f(a+qh)f(a+ph)−f(a+qh), add and subtract f(a)f(a)f(a):

f(a+ph)−f(a+qh)h⟶(p−q)f′(a).\boxed{\frac{f(a+ph)-f(a+qh)}h\longrightarrow(p-q)f'(a)}.hf(a+ph)−f(a+qh)​⟶(p−q)f′(a)​.

This uses differentiability at aaa alone. It does not assume f′f'f′ exists or is continuous at nearby points.

Concept C15 — L'Hôpital's rule: useful only after its checks

This is a supporting alternative, not the foundation of the standard-limit proofs. Learn the ordinary derivative rules in Chapter 10 before using it independently.

For a quotient f(x)/g(x)f(x)/g(x)f(x)/g(x) with an actual 0/00/00/0 or ∞/∞\infty/\infty∞/∞ limiting form, a standard version of the rule allows

lim⁡f(x)g(x)=lim⁡f′(x)g′(x)\boxed{\lim\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} =\lim\frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)}}limg(x)f(x)​=limg′(x)f′(x)​​

provided f,gf,gf,g are differentiable on the relevant nearby punctured interval, ggg and g′g'g′ are nonzero there, and the derivative-ratio limit exists (finite or extended). Treat each side separately when required. A limit may exist even if this method does not apply.

It is not the quotient differentiation formula. We are comparing two limits, not saying f/g=f′/g′f/g=f'/g'f/g=f′/g′ at each input.

For example,

lim⁡x→0ex−1−xx2 =rule lim⁡x→0ex−12x=12.\lim_{x\to0}\frac{e^x-1-x}{x^2} \ \overset{\text{rule}}=\ \lim_{x\to0}\frac{e^x-1}{2x} =\frac12.x→0lim​x2ex−1−x​ =rule x→0lim​2xex−1​=21​.

After the first application the new quotient is still 0/00/00/0, so another valid application would also work. The expansion ex=1+x+x2/2+O(x3)e^x=1+x+x^2/2+O(x^3)ex=1+x+x2/2+O(x3) is shorter once that pattern is familiar.

Do not use it automatically:

  • Rewrite 1∞1^\infty1∞ using logs; it is not a quotient yet.
  • Rewrite ∞−∞\infty-\infty∞−∞ using algebra first.
  • For Q15 the unknown function is only known to be differentiable at one point. Its nearby derivative assumptions are not supplied.
  • For the oscillation in Q29, a squeeze is direct and reliable.
  • Do not prove sin⁡x/x→1\sin x/x\to1sinx/x→1 by using a derivative formula whose own proof used that same limit.

Choose the route from the clue

Visible clue First useful move Why
Denominator stays nonzero Substitute Continuity already gives the answer
Polynomial 0/00/00/0 Factor Removes a common zero
Root difference Conjugate / difference of cubes Keeps the small surviving difference
Sine/tangent at a small angle Match angle with denominator Preserves scale factors
Earlier Taylor terms subtracted Keep the first surviving order Prevents false cancellation to zero
Variable power Take the log of the whole expression Changes the exponent into a product
Floor of a large argument Bound the rounding error Staircase detail becomes unnecessary
Bounded oscillation times a small factor Squeeze Bounds may converge even when sine does not
Sum of neighbouring reciprocal products Partial fractions / telescope Almost all finite terms cancel
Width 1/n1/n1/n and argument r/nr/nr/n Rectangle sum Many small terms can give a finite area
Unknown differentiable function at one point Build difference quotients there Uses exactly the assumption supplied

Worked solutions to the 30 PDF questions

Try the question first. Then read the clue and the reason for the method before following the calculation. Use each graph to understand the behaviour; use the equation or bound to prove the answer.

Question 1 — Make each small angle match its own denominator

PDF page 43 | MCQ | Notes: C05

lim⁡x→0sin⁡5xtan⁡3x\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin5x}{\tan3x}x→0lim​tan3xsin5x​ is equal to

  • (a) 35\dfrac3553​
  • (b) 111
  • (c) 53\dfrac5335​
  • (d) 151515

Both angles are small, but their sizes are different. Did you notice the 5x5x5x and 3x3x3x? The standard result needs the same small angle in numerator and denominator:

sin⁡5xtan⁡3x=sin⁡5x5x 3xtan⁡3x 53.\frac{\sin5x}{\tan3x} =\frac{\sin5x}{5x}\, \frac{3x}{\tan3x}\,\frac53.tan3xsin5x​=5xsin5x​tan3x3x​35​.

The first two factors tend to 111 in radians. Thus the answer is 5/3\boxed{5/3}5/3​, option (c).

Why substitution stops: at x=0x=0x=0 it gives 0/00/00/0, not a value. Another possible approach: use sin⁡5x=5x+O(x3)\sin5x=5x+O(x^3)sin5x=5x+O(x3) and tan⁡3x=3x+O(x3)\tan3x=3x+O(x^3)tan3x=3x+O(x3). Their ratio tends to 5/35/35/3. Matching the standard limits needs less expansion.

Question 2 — The cosine difference starts at the square term

PDF page 43 | Numerical value | Notes: C05

lim⁡x→01−cos⁡4xx2=\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{1-\cos4x}{x^2}=x→0lim​x21−cos4x​= ____.

A cosine difference suggests the half-angle identity.

1−cos⁡4x=2sin⁡2(2x).1-\cos4x=2\sin^2(2x).1−cos4x=2sin2(2x).

So

1−cos⁡4xx2=8(sin⁡2x2x)2⟶8.\frac{1-\cos4x}{x^2} =8\left(\frac{\sin2x}{2x}\right)^2 \longrightarrow\boxed{8}.x21−cos4x​=8(2xsin2x​)2⟶8​.

Check the factor: the angle coefficient is 444, so the general result gives 42/2=84^2/2=842/2=8, not 4/24/24/2.

Another possible approach: cos⁡4x=1−(4x)2/2+O(x4)\cos4x=1-(4x)^2/2+O(x^4)cos4x=1−(4x)2/2+O(x4), giving numerator 8x2+O(x4)8x^2+O(x^4)8x2+O(x4). Dividing by x2x^2x2 gives the same limit.

Question 3 — Keep the first terms that do not cancel

PDF page 43 | Numerical value | Notes: C07

lim⁡x→0ex−e−x−2xx−sin⁡x=\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{e^x-e^{-x}-2x}{x-\sin x}=x→0lim​x−sinxex−e−x−2x​= ____.

The subtraction tells us how far to expand. The two exponentials cancel their even powers. Subtracting 2x2x2x then removes the linear term. The numerator starts at x3x^3x3, not xxx:

ex−e−x−2x=2(x+x36+x5120)−2x+O(x7)=x33+x560+O(x7),x−sin⁡x=x36−x5120+O(x7).\begin{aligned} e^x-e^{-x}-2x &=2\left(x+\frac{x^3}{6}+\frac{x^5}{120}\right)-2x+O(x^7)\\ &=\frac{x^3}{3}+\frac{x^5}{60}+O(x^7),\\ x-\sin x&=\frac{x^3}{6}-\frac{x^5}{120}+O(x^7). \end{aligned}ex−e−x−2xx−sinx​=2(x+6x3​+120x5​)−2x+O(x7)=3x3​+60x5​+O(x7),=6x3​−120x5​+O(x7).​

Cancel x3x^3x3 for nearby x≠0x\ne0x=0:

1/3+x2/60+O(x4)1/6−x2/120+O(x4)⟶2.\frac{1/3+x^2/60+O(x^4)} {1/6-x^2/120+O(x^4)} \longrightarrow\boxed{2}.1/6−x2/120+O(x4)1/3+x2/60+O(x4)​⟶2​.

Using only ex≈1+xe^x\approx1+xex≈1+x and sin⁡x≈x\sin x\approx xsinx≈x would leave another 0/00/00/0 and lose the answer.

Another possible approach: after checking smoothness and nonzero denominator derivatives near 000, three applications of L'Hôpital give (ex+e−x)/cos⁡x→2(e^x+e^{-x})/\cos x\to2(ex+e−x)/cosx→2. The expansion shows the cancellation order more directly.

Question 4 — A base near one and a large exponent

PDF page 43 | MCQ | Notes: C08

lim⁡x→∞(1+3x)2x\displaystyle\lim_{x\to\infty}\left(1+\frac3x\right)^{2x}x→∞lim​(1+x3​)2x equals

  • (a) e6e^6e6
  • (b) e3/2e^{3/2}e3/2
  • (c) e2/3e^{2/3}e2/3
  • (d) e3e^3e3

The base approaches one while the exponent grows. Put u=3/xu=3/xu=3/x. Then u→0+u\to0^+u→0+ and 2x=6/u2x=6/u2x=6/u:

(1+3x)2x=((1+u)1/u)6⟶e6.\left(1+\frac3x\right)^{2x} =\left((1+u)^{1/u}\right)^6 \longrightarrow e^6.(1+x3​)2x=((1+u)1/u)6⟶e6.

Thus e6\boxed{e^6}e6​, option (a).

Another possible approach: for the positive expression YYY, ln⁡Y=2xln⁡(1+3/x)=6 ln⁡(1+3/x)/(3/x)→6\ln Y=2x\ln(1+3/x)=6\,\ln(1+3/x)/(3/x)\to6lnY=2xln(1+3/x)=6ln(1+3/x)/(3/x)→6. Question 5 — A number below one raised to a large power

PDF page 43 | MCQ | Notes: C08

lim⁡x→0(cos⁡x)1/x2\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}(\cos x)^{1/x^2}x→0lim​(cosx)1/x2 equals

  • (a) e1/2e^{1/2}e1/2

  • (c) e−2e^{-2}e−2

Let Y=(cos⁡x)1/x2Y=(\cos x)^{1/x^2}Y=(cosx)1/x2. Its base is positive nearby, so

ln⁡Y=ln⁡cos⁡xx2⟶−12.\ln Y=\frac{\ln\cos x}{x^2}\longrightarrow-\frac12.lnY=x2lncosx​⟶−21​.

Hence Y→e−1/2\boxed{Y\to e^{-1/2}}Y→e−1/2​, option (d).

Question 6 — Rewrite the base as one plus a small amount

PDF page 43 | MCQ | Notes: C08

lim⁡x→∞(x2+1x2−1)x2\displaystyle\lim_{x\to\infty}\left(\frac{x^2+1}{x^2-1}\right)^{x^2}x→∞lim​(x2−1x2+1​)x2 equals

  • (a) eee
  • (b) e2e^2e2
  • (c) e−2e^{-2}e−2
  • (d) 111

Question 23 — A triple-angle identity removes cancellation

PDF page 45 | Numerical value | Notes: C05,C07

lim⁡x→03sin⁡x−sin⁡3xx−sin⁡x=\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{3\sin x-\sin3x}{x-\sin x}=x→0lim​x−sinx3sinx−sin3x​= ____.

sin⁡3x=3sin⁡x−4sin⁡3x⇒3sin⁡x−sin⁡3x=4sin⁡3x.\sin3x=3\sin x-4\sin^3x \quad\Rightarrow\quad 3\sin x-\sin3x=4\sin^3x.sin3x=3sinx−4sin3x⇒3sinx−sin3x=4sin3x.

3sin⁡x−sin⁡3xx−sin⁡x=4(sin⁡x/x)3(x−sin⁡x)/x3⟶41/6=24.\frac{3\sin x-\sin3x}{x-\sin x} =\frac{4(\sin x/x)^3}{(x-\sin x)/x^3} \longrightarrow\frac4{1/6}=\boxed{24}.x−sinx3sinx−sin3x​=(x−sinx)/x34(sinx/x)3​⟶1/64​=24​.

Question 24 — Subtract a product by breaking it into three differences

PDF page 45 | Numerical value | Notes: C05,C07

A product near one can be split without multiplying three series. Use

Question 25 — Write each fraction as a difference

PDF page 45 | MCQ | Notes: C12

lim⁡n→∞[11⋅3+13⋅5+⋯+1(2n−1)(2n+1)]\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\left[\frac1{1\cdot3}+\frac1{3\cdot5}+\cdots+\frac1{(2n-1)(2n+1)}\right]n→∞lim​[1⋅31​+3⋅51​+⋯+(2n−1)(2n+1)1​] equals

Question 26 — Use the difference-of-cubes identity

Coverage and source notes

All 303030 supplied questions appear in order: 212121 MCQs and 999 numerical-value questions. Independent calculations agree with the intended source answers. The notes explicitly handle radians, real domains, one-sided limits, cancellation orders and sequence-sum normalization.

Q10/Q11 include their small rectangle-sum prerequisite. Q15 uses differentiability at the given point alone, without assuming nearby derivatives. L'Hôpital is a checked supporting alternative; it is not used circularly to establish the foundational trig limit.
